title: Least subobject generated by a subset of a finite fibre
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], and let $\mathcal A$ be an essentially small $k$-linear abelian category [def-sp-abelian]: its isomorphism classes form a set, its Hom sets are $k$-vector spaces, and composition is bilinear. Let $F:\mathcal A\to\operatorname{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}}_k$ be a $k$-linear faithful functor preserving short exact sequences, where faithful means injective on each Hom set and finite-dimensional means having a finite spanning set [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. For $V\in\mathcal A$ and any subset $S\subseteq F(V)$, there is a monomorphism $i:G\hookrightarrow V$ such that $S\subseteq\operatorname{im}F(i)$ and such that, for every monomorphism $j:H\hookrightarrow V$ with $S\subseteq\operatorname{im}F(j)$, there is a unique morphism $a:G\to H$ satisfying $j\circ a=i$. Thus $i$ is the least subobject of $V$ whose fibre contains $S$, unique up to a unique isomorphism over $V$. A subobject here means a monomorphism into $V$, with two such monomorphisms identified when they are isomorphic over $V$. The subset $S$ may be empty and $V$ may be zero.

source.place: Section 9(d), printed p.175, paragraphs on the subobject lattice and “Let X be an object of C and S a subset of omega(X)”; the asserted smallest generated subobject, immediately before Lemma 9.33. Finite-dimensional fibres avoid requiring arbitrary limits.

proof.text: We first record the elementary cancellation argument behind Milne's reflection assertion. If $F(u)$ is invertible, cancellation after applying $F$ and injectivity on Hom sets show that $u$ is both mono and epi. By [def-sp-abelian], write $u:A\to B$ as a kernel of $v:B\to C$. Since $vu=0$ and $u$ is epi, $v=0$. The kernel property applied to $1_B$ gives $s:B\to A$ with $us=1_B$; cancellation by $u$ gives $su=1_A$. Thus $u$ is invertible. Also $F$ is additive by $k$-linearity, so [lem-sp-exact-functor-preserves-homology] applies: it preserves monomorphisms, kernels, cokernels and finite limits and colimits.

source.place: Section 9(d), printed p.175 (PDF p.187), subobject-lattice paragraph and footnote 6; paragraph defining the subobject generated by S immediately before Lemma 9.33.

proof.text: Consider the nonempty subset of $\mathbf N$ consisting of $\dim_k F(H)$ for monomorphisms $j:H\hookrightarrow V$ whose fibre image contains $S$. Dimension is [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]; every $F(H)$ is finite-dimensional by hypothesis. The identity of $V$ is a candidate. Choose a candidate $i:G\hookrightarrow V$ realizing the least such integer $d$. This uses leastness in $\mathbf N$, not an infinite intersection or the existence of arbitrary limits.

source.place: Section 9(d), printed p.175 (PDF p.187), subobject-lattice paragraph and footnote 6; paragraph defining the subobject generated by S immediately before Lemma 9.33.

proof.text: Fix another candidate $j:H\hookrightarrow V$. Form the kernel $P\to G\oplus H$ of $(i,-j):G\oplus H\to V$, using the kernels and finite biproducts in [def-sp-abelian]; write its components $p:P\to G$, $q:P\to H$. Thus $ip=jq$. The morphism $p$ is mono: equality after $p$ implies equality after $q$ by cancellation by $j$, hence equality into $G\oplus H$, hence equality into $P$ by the kernel monomorphism. The same argument makes $q$ mono, and $ip$ is mono. By [lem-sp-exact-functor-preserves-homology], $F$ preserves this kernel and biproduct, identifying $F(P)$ with the pairs $(x,y)$ satisfying $F(i)x=F(j)y$. For every $s\in S$ choose lifts $x,y$ under $F(i),F(j)$; their pair lies in this kernel. Therefore $S\subseteq\operatorname{im}F(ip)$, and minimality gives $d\leq\dim_k F(P)$.

source.place: Section 9(d), printed p.175 (PDF p.187), subobject-lattice paragraph and footnote 6; paragraph defining the subobject generated by S immediately before Lemma 9.33.

proof.text: Put $Q=\operatorname{coker}p$. The preservation statement (a) of [lem-sp-exact-functor-preserves-homology] gives the short exact vector-space sequence $0\to F(P)\xrightarrow{F(p)}F(G)\to F(Q)\to0$. All three spaces are finite-dimensional because they are fibres of objects of $\mathcal A$. By [lem-trf-finite-dimensional-short-exact-dimension], $d=\dim_k F(P)+\dim_k F(Q)$. Together with the preceding inequality this forces $\dim_k F(Q)=0$. By [def-weil-vector-space-dimension], a zero-dimensional space has an empty basis and is zero. Thus $F(p)$ is injective with zero cokernel, hence bijective: its image is the whole target by exactness. Step 1 now makes $p$ invertible.

source.place: Section 9(d), printed p.175 (PDF p.187), subobject-lattice paragraph and footnote 6; paragraph defining the subobject generated by S immediately before Lemma 9.33.

proof.text: Define $a=q p^{-1}:G\to H$. The relation $ip=jq$ gives $ja=i$. If $ja'=i$ also, cancellation by the monomorphism $j$ gives $a'=a$. This proves leastness with the required unique factorization. For two least candidates the unique arrows in both directions compose to identities, by the same uniqueness, giving a unique isomorphism over $V$. The construction works for $S=\varnothing$ (all subobjects are candidates) and for $V=0$; neither the minimum argument nor the dimension formula requires positive dimension.

source.place: Section 9(d), printed p.175 (PDF p.187), subobject-lattice paragraph and footnote 6; paragraph defining the subobject generated by S immediately before Lemma 9.33.

Its statement matches Milne iAG2017 §9(d), printed p.175 (PDF p.187), hypothesis by hypothesis: an essentially small k-linear abelian category, a k-linear exact faithful functor to finite-dimensional vector spaces, and the smallest subobject whose fibre contains S. It is not weakened. Milne assumes this intersection exists without proof; the split supplies it in five correct steps. Step 1: faithfulness reflects mono, epi and iso, using that every mono is a kernel (def-sp-abelian) and exactness node (a). Step 2: choose a candidate of least fibre dimension (the identity of V is a candidate). Step 3: take P = ker((i,-j): G⊕H→V); I checked that p is mono; F preserves the kernel and the biproduct, so F(P) = {(x,y): F(i)x = F(j)y} and ip is again a candidate. Step 4: F gives a short exact sequence 0→F(P)→F(G)→F(Q)→0; with dimension additivity this forces F(Q) = 0, so F(p) is bijective and step 1 makes p an isomorphism. Step 5: unique factorization by mono cancellation, so the least subobject is unique up to unique isomorphism over V. Small cases checked: S empty, V = 0, S = {0}, S = F(V), the identity functor on vector spaces (gives the linear span), and finite-dimensional comodules (gives the smallest subcomodule).
